title: Year three opens: after Moses
hook: the Prophets are the second part of the Tanakh; they begin the day Moses dies
carry: the story goes on without moses

segments.voice: Yesterday, chazak, and a room calling out be strong at the end of a book. Your line was the torah, the prayer, the year. Did you tell someone one thing you learned? Today, year three begins. Day six hundred ninety-seven.

After the death of Moses. Those are the first words of the next book. Not a new world, not a fresh start: a death, right at the top of the page. Most new books start by introducing someone. This one starts by saying who is gone, and only then turns to the man left standing: Joshua son of Nun, who had served Moses. One sentence holds the old leader and the new one. The Torah has an ending. The people's story doesn't. This year we walk on, into the second part of the Bible.
screen: `AFTER THE DEATH OF MOSES.` → `WHO IS GONE, WHO IS LEFT.` → `THE STORY GOES ON.`

segments.voice: Jews call their Bible the Tanakh. The name is built from the first letters of its three parts: Torah, the teaching; Nevi'im, the Prophets; Ketuvim, the Writings. Year one and year two read through the first part. Now the second. Nevi'im is the plural of navi, prophet. And the first surprise is what's in it. Before the books of prophets who speak in poetry, Nevi'im opens with books that read like history: Joshua, Judges, Samuel, Kings. Jewish tradition calls them the Former Prophets. Battles, judges, kings, betrayals, a people trying to live in a land with the Torah in its hands. So why call history prophecy? The Torah gives a clue. When Moses protests that he can't speak well enough to face Pharaoh, God answers: "Aaron thy brother shall be thy prophet." There, a navi is a spokesman, the one who carries words from one person to another. In that sense a prophet isn't mainly a fortune teller. A prophet is someone a message travels through. And these books carry their message through what happens: when the people keep faith, when they don't, and what follows. Then the second surprise is how it starts. "Moses My servant is dead." That's God, speaking to Joshua, in the book's second verse. No long scene of grief; the Torah already gave the mourning its days. A plain sentence, and then straight on: arise, cross this Jordan. The teacher of the whole Torah is gone, and the story doesn't stop. It goes on with someone new, in a harder place. That's the shape of the year ahead: a people, after Moses, working it out.
screen: `TORAH, NEVI'IM, KETUVIM.` · `IT OPENS WITH HISTORY: THE FORMER PROPHETS.` · `A NAVI CARRIES A MESSAGE.` · then, large: `MOSES MY SERVANT IS DEAD.` · then: `THE STORY GOES ON.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: read Joshua 1:1. If there's a Bible near you, open it to the first page after Deuteronomy. If not, hear it in plain words: after the death of Moses, the servant of the Lord, the Lord spoke to Joshua son of Nun, who had served Moses. Read it once, slowly. Then keep only four words: after the death of. Let them bring to mind someone whose work you now carry on, a parent, a teacher, a friend. Hold them for a while, and what they handed you. The bell holds the time.
Nevi'im. The Prophets, the second part of the Tanakh, opening with Joshua and the books that tell the story as history. Today's word.
Your line: the story goes on without moses. Today, notice one thing someone else started that you're now carrying on. Day six hundred ninety-seven.

howItsDone: In synagogues, each Shabbat Torah reading is followed by a haftarah, a passage from the Prophets; on Simchat Torah, as the Torah ends with Moses' death, the haftarah is commonly the opening of the book of Joshua.

fork.setup: you're Joshua. Moses, who led the people through the whole Torah, has died. God speaks to you for the first time in your new role. what comes next?
options: more time to mourn before anything else.
an order to cross the Jordan now.
a promise that another Moses will come.
fork.reveal: "Moses My servant is dead," and straight on: arise, cross this Jordan. the mourning already happened in Deuteronomy. the story doesn't wait.

what it means: Nevi'im, the second part of the Tanakh, opens with history: Joshua, Judges, Samuel and Kings, the Former Prophets.
what a scholar hears: navi as spokesman. in Exodus 7:1, Aaron is Moses' navi, the one who carries his words to Pharaoh.

notes: Verify the exact JPS 1917 wording of Joshua 1:2 ('Moses My servant is dead', with capitalized divine pronoun) and Exodus 7:1 ('Aaron thy brother shall be thy prophet').
Haftarah for Simchat Torah: Joshua 1 (Ashkenazi 1:1–18, Sephardi 1:1–9 by common custom). Script says 'in synagogues'; confirm the custom's spread.
Tanakh as an acronym of Torah, Nevi'im, Ketuvim is stated as fact (a naming convention, not an etymology); confirm phrasing.
Navi as 'spokesman' is drawn from Exodus 7:1 only; no lexical claim about the root is made.
'Former Prophets' for Joshua–Kings is standard Jewish usage (Nevi'im Rishonim); no count of books is given.
